---
title: "quarto-lock"
subtitle: "Password-lock Quarto sites on static hosting"
---

# A cryptographic lock for Quarto

`quarto-lock` protects a rendered Quarto website or book on static hosting by encrypting its local output at build time and decrypting it in the visitor's browser only after the shared password is entered.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try this demo"}
This repository is intentionally configured with a **public demo password**:

**`quarto-lock-demo`**

Use it on the lock screen to open the deployed example.
:::

> [!WARNING]
> `quarto-lock-demo` is deliberately public and must **never** be reused for real protected content. In your own project, provide a strong private password through the `QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD` environment variable or a GitHub Actions secret.

## What is protected?

The lock is applied after Quarto renders the project. Local HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts, search indexes, JSON files, PDFs, ZIP files, and other local downloads can therefore be encrypted together.

The public host receives ciphertext (`*.qlock`) plus the small runtime required to display the lock screen and decrypt resources in the browser.

```text
private Quarto source
        |
        | quarto render
        v
      _site/
        |
        | quarto-lock post-render
        v
encrypted static site
        |
        v
GitHub Pages / any static host
        |
        v
      🔒 password
        |
        v
content decrypted in the browser
```

## Install

From a Quarto project:

```bash
quarto add lsbjordao/quarto-lock
```

Then enable the extension in `_quarto.yml`:

```yaml
filters:
  - quarto-lock
```

For a real project, render with a private password:

```bash
export QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD='replace-this-with-a-strong-passphrase'
quarto render
```

The password is used only during the locking step. It is not written to the generated HTML, JavaScript, or encrypted payloads.

## Customize or translate the lock screen

The default interface is English, but the complete lock screen can be translated or reworded without editing the extension source.

Copy the supplied configuration template:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

Then edit `.env`:

```dotenv
QUARTO_LOCK_LANG=en
QUARTO_LOCK_TITLE="Protected content"
QUARTO_LOCK_MESSAGE="Enter the password to unlock this content."
QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD_LABEL="Password"
QUARTO_LOCK_BUTTON_LABEL="Unlock"
QUARTO_LOCK_FOOTER="Protected by Quarto Lock"
QUARTO_LOCK_ERROR_INCORRECT="Incorrect password."
QUARTO_LOCK_ERROR_SECURE_CONTEXT="This site must be opened over HTTPS (or localhost)."
```

For example, Portuguese can be configured with:

```dotenv
QUARTO_LOCK_LANG=pt-BR
QUARTO_LOCK_TITLE="Área reservada"
QUARTO_LOCK_MESSAGE="Digite a senha para abrir este conteúdo."
QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD_LABEL="Senha"
QUARTO_LOCK_BUTTON_LABEL="Entrar"
QUARTO_LOCK_FOOTER="Protegido por Quarto Lock"
QUARTO_LOCK_ERROR_INCORRECT="Senha incorreta."
QUARTO_LOCK_ERROR_SECURE_CONTEXT="Este site precisa ser aberto por HTTPS (ou localhost)."
```

`quarto-lock` reads `.env` automatically from the project root. Existing environment variables and GitHub Actions Secrets take precedence, so the recommended pattern is:

```text
.env                     → UI text / language
QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD     → shell or GitHub Actions Secret
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Keep real passwords out of Git"}
This repository commits `.env.example` but ignores `.env`. The UI text is not secret, but `.env` files commonly accumulate credentials over time, so keeping the working file out of version control is safer.
:::

See **Customize UI** in the navigation for all available strings, configuration precedence, and another language example.

## Test a locked build locally

Normal `quarto preview` is intentionally **not locked**. Quarto preview performs incremental renders, while `quarto-lock` replaces the clear rendered output with encrypted payloads.

Use a full render and then serve `_site` directly:

```bash
export QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD='replace-this-with-a-strong-passphrase'
quarto render
python3 -m http.server 3073 -d _site
```

Then open <http://127.0.0.1:3073/>.

For this repository's demo:

```bash
npm run preview:locked
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Do not run quarto preview after locking"}
Running `quarto preview` after `quarto render` renders the project again in preview mode and recreates clear HTML in `_site`. To inspect a locked build, serve `_site` directly instead.
:::

# Publishing with GitHub

`quarto-lock` is especially useful with GitHub because the **source repository and the published static site do not need to be the same repository**.

That distinction matters for private projects.

According to the [GitHub Pages documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/creating-a-github-pages-site), GitHub Pages is available from public repositories on GitHub Free. Publishing Pages directly from a private repository requires GitHub Pro, Team, Enterprise Cloud, or Enterprise Server. Even when the source repository is private, the resulting GitHub Pages site is normally public on the internet.

Therefore there are two useful deployment patterns.

## Option 1 — Pages from the same repository

This is the simplest option when:

- the repository is public; or
- your GitHub plan supports Pages from private repositories.

Create this structure in the Quarto repository:

```text
.github/
└── workflows/
    └── publish.yml
```

You can create it from the terminal with:

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
```

Then create `.github/workflows/publish.yml`:

```yaml
name: Publish locked Quarto site

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    env:
      QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD }}

    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - name: Set up Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: "22"

      - name: Set up Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      - name: Render and publish locked site
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
        with:
          target: gh-pages
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD }}
```

The workflow renders Quarto inside GitHub Actions. The `quarto-lock` post-render hook then encrypts the output before the generated site is pushed to the `gh-pages` branch.

### Add the password as a GitHub Actions secret

In the source repository, open:

**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**

Create:

```text
Name: QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD
Secret: your-long-private-passphrase
```

Do **not** put a real password directly in `_quarto.yml`, `index.qmd`, JavaScript, or the workflow YAML.

This repository is intentionally different because `quarto-lock-demo` is a public demonstration password.

## Option 2 — private source → Actions → separate public Pages repository

This is the recommended GitHub Free workflow when the Quarto source itself must remain private.

```text
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│ PRIVATE repository            │
│                               │
│ *.qmd                         │
│ data                          │
│ source code                   │
│ _extensions/quarto-lock       │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                │
                │ GitHub Actions
                │ QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD secret
                ▼
         quarto render
                │
         quarto-lock encrypts
                │
                ▼
┌───────────────────────────────┐
│ PUBLIC Pages repository       │
│                               │
│ index.html  ← lock screen     │
│ *.qlock     ← ciphertext      │
│ lock runtime                  │
└───────────────┬───────────────┘
                │
                ▼
          GitHub Pages
```

The public repository never needs the `.qmd` source, datasets, notebooks, scripts, or the password. It receives only the already-rendered, already-encrypted `_site` output.

### 1. Keep your Quarto repository private

For example:

```text
your-user/private-report
```

It contains the real project:

```text
private-report/
├── .github/
│   └── workflows/
│       └── publish.yml
├── _extensions/
│   └── quarto-lock/
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd
├── chapters/
└── data/
```

### 2. Create a second, public repository only for the encrypted site

For example:

```text
your-user/private-report-pages
```

This repository may be public because it will contain only the locked build.

If you want a user site at `https://your-user.github.io/`, use a public repository named:

```text
your-user.github.io
```

For a project site, any public repository name can be used and the default URL will normally include the repository name.

### 3. Create a deployment token

Create a **fine-grained personal access token** with access only to the public destination repository and grant it permission to write repository contents.

Store that token as a secret in the **private source repository**:

**Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**

```text
PAGES_DEPLOY_TOKEN
```

Also create:

```text
QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD
```

The two secrets have different purposes:

| Secret | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD` | derives the encryption key used to lock the Quarto output |
| `PAGES_DEPLOY_TOKEN` | allows the private repository's Action to push the encrypted output to the public repository |

### 4. Create `.github/workflows/publish.yml`

Inside the **private source repository**:

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
```

Create `.github/workflows/publish.yml` with the following content. Replace `YOUR-USER/YOUR-PUBLIC-PAGES-REPO` with the destination repository.

```yaml
name: Publish locked Quarto site

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    env:
      QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.QUARTO_LOCK_PASSWORD }}

    steps:
      - name: Check out private Quarto source
        uses: actions/checkout@v6

      - name: Set up Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: "22"

      - name: Set up Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

      - name: Render and lock site
        run: quarto render

      - name: Check out public Pages repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          repository: YOUR-USER/YOUR-PUBLIC-PAGES-REPO
          token: ${{ secrets.PAGES_DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
          path: pages-target

      - name: Copy encrypted site to gh-pages branch
        shell: bash
        run: |
          cd pages-target
          git checkout -B gh-pages
          find . -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -name .git -exec rm -rf {} +
          cp -a "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/_site/." .
          touch .nojekyll

          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add -A

          if ! git diff --cached --quiet; then
            git commit -m "Publish locked Quarto site"
          fi

          git push --force origin gh-pages
```

The critical ordering is:

```text
quarto render
      ↓
quarto-lock encrypts _site
      ↓
copy _site to public repository
      ↓
publish
```

The workflow must **never copy the Quarto source repository itself** to the public destination.

### 5. Enable Pages in the public destination repository

Open the **public Pages repository** and go to:

**Settings → Pages**

Choose:

```text
Source: Deploy from a branch
Branch: gh-pages
Folder: /(root)
```

GitHub documents both branch-based publication and custom GitHub Actions workflows as supported Pages publishing sources. See [Configuring a publishing source](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/configuring-a-publishing-source-for-your-github-pages-site) and [Using custom workflows with GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/using-custom-workflows-with-github-pages).

### 6. Push normally

From then on:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Update report"
git push
```

causes:

```text
push to private repo
        ↓
GitHub Action starts
        ↓
Quarto renders
        ↓
quarto-lock encrypts
        ↓
encrypted _site pushed to public repo
        ↓
GitHub Pages updates
```

Your collaborators can receive the Pages URL and the shared password without receiving access to the private source repository.

## Which GitHub setup should I use?

| Situation | Recommended setup |
|---|---|
| Public Quarto repository | Same repository + `gh-pages` |
| Private repository with GitHub plan that supports private Pages | Same repository + `gh-pages` |
| Private repository on GitHub Free | **Private source repo → Actions → separate public Pages repo** |
| Highly sensitive content requiring individual identities or revocation | Use server-side authentication instead of `quarto-lock` |

The third option is particularly useful because GitHub Pages remains a static host while GitHub Actions becomes the trusted build boundary: the Action temporarily receives the secret, performs the encryption, and publishes only ciphertext.

# Why “lock”, not “login”?

This is not an account system. There are no users, password recovery, roles, MFA, or server-side sessions.

It is client-side cryptographic access control designed for static hosting:

- anyone may download the encrypted payload;
- a strong shared password is required to decrypt it;
- the password is not embedded in the published files;
- changing the password requires rendering and publishing again;
- once a visitor unlocks the content, that visitor can still copy or save it.

For highly sensitive or regulated material, use server-side identity and authentication instead.

# Security summary

`quarto-lock` currently uses:

- PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256;
- 600,000 iterations by default;
- AES-256-GCM;
- a random salt per build;
- a unique random IV per protected file;
- authenticated ciphertext;
- Web Crypto for browser-side key derivation and decryption.

The important deployment principle is simple:

> **Secrets enter the build; only ciphertext leaves the build.**
